prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A quantum critical point (QCP) between the antiferromagnetic and the paramagnetic phases was realized by applying a hydrostatic pressure of ~ 7 GPa on single crystals of NiS_{2} pyrite with a low residual resistivity, rho_{0}, of 0.5 mu-Omega-cm. We found that the critical behavior of the resistivity, rho, in this clean system contrasts sharply with those observed in its disordered analogue, NiS_{2-x}Se_{x} solid-solution, demonstrating the unexpectedly drastic effect of disorder on the quantum criticality. Over a whole paramagnetic region investigated up to P = 9 GPa, a crossover temperature, defined as the onset of T^{2} dependence of rho, an indication of Fermi liquid, was suppressed to a substantially low temperature T sim 2 K and, instead, a non Fermi liquid behavior of rho, T^{3/2}-dependence, robustly showed up.

outputs.L1: A quantum critical point (QCP) between the antiferromagnetic and paramagnetic phases was realized by applying a hydrostatic pressure of approximately 7 GPa to single crystals of pyrite NiS\(_2\) with a low residual resistivity, \(\rho_0\), of 0.5 \(\mu\Omega\)-cm. We found that the critical behavior of the resistivity, \(\rho\), in this clean system contrasts sharply with that observed in its disordered analogue, the NiS\(_{2-x}\)Se\(_x\) solid solution, demonstrating the unexpectedly pronounced effect of disorder on quantum criticality. Across the entire paramagnetic region investigated, up to \(P = 9\) GPa, the crossover temperature—defined as the onset of the \(T^2\) dependence of \(\rho\), indicative of a Fermi liquid—was suppressed to a substantially low temperature of \(T \sim 2\) K. Instead, non-Fermi-liquid behavior of \(\rho\), characterized by a robust \(T^{3/2}\) dependence, emerged.
outputs.L2: A quantum critical point (QCP) separating the antiferromagnetic state from the paramagnetic state was produced by subjecting high-purity single-crystal NiS₂ pyrite to hydrostatic pressure of about 7 GPa; the crystals had a small residual resistivity, ρ₀, of 0.5 μΩ·cm. In this clean material, the critical behavior of the electrical resistivity, ρ, was found to be very different from that reported for the more disordered counterpart, the NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ solid solution, revealing that disorder has a surprisingly strong influence on quantum critical behavior. Throughout the paramagnetic pressure range examined, extending up to P = 9 GPa, the crossover temperature marking the appearance of the T² dependence of ρ—characteristic of a Fermi liquid—was pushed down to a very low value of roughly T ≈ 2 K. Instead, non-Fermi-liquid behavior, expressed as a robust T³ᐟ² dependence of ρ, was clearly observed.
outputs.L3:
A quantum critical point between antiferromagnetic and paramagnetic phases was realized in clean NiS₂ pyrite single crystals by applying hydrostatic pressure of approximately 7 GPa. The high quality of these crystals was reflected in their very low residual resistivity of about 0.5 μΩ-cm, indicating that the system was exceptionally clean and largely free from disorder-related scattering.

The critical behavior of the resistivity in clean NiS₂ was found to differ sharply from that observed in the disordered analogue NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ. This distinction is significant because it shows that the presence of disorder can fundamentally alter the nature of quantum critical behavior. In other words, the comparison between clean NiS₂ and the more disordered selenium-substituted compound demonstrates that disorder has a drastic effect on quantum criticality near the antiferromagnetic-to-paramagnetic phase boundary.

Furthermore, throughout the investigated paramagnetic pressure range, extending up to 9 GPa, conventional Fermi-liquid behavior was strongly suppressed, persisting only down to temperatures of around 2 K. Instead, a robust non-Fermi-liquid resistivity behavior proportional to T³ᐟ² emerged over a broad region. These results indicate that clean NiS₂ under pressure provides an important platform for studying quantum criticality in a low-disorder antiferromagnetic metal and highlight the crucial role of disorder in shaping the transport properties near quantum phase transitions.
outputs.L4:
A quantum critical point separating antiferromagnetic and paramagnetic metallic phases was investigated in clean, high-quality single-crystal NiS₂ under nearly hydrostatic pressure of approximately 7 GPa. Low-temperature electrical resistivity measurements were used to track the evolution of charge transport as the antiferromagnetic ordering temperature was continuously suppressed by pressure toward zero. This approach allowed the intrinsic behavior of the pressure-tuned transition to be examined without introducing the chemical disorder that is unavoidable in substitutionally tuned systems.

The results show that, near the critical pressure, the resistivity deviates strongly from the conventional Fermi-liquid form. Instead of following the usual low-temperature dependence ρ = ρ₀ + AT², expected for a normal metal dominated by electron-electron scattering, the clean pressurized NiS₂ crystals exhibit a robust non-Fermi-liquid power law, approximately ρ = ρ₀ + AT³ᐟ², over an extended temperature range. The temperature below which Fermi-liquid behavior is recovered is strongly suppressed near the quantum critical point, indicating that critical magnetic fluctuations dominate the electronic scattering down to very low temperatures.

These observations demonstrate that the intrinsic quantum critical behavior of clean NiS₂ differs markedly from that found in the chemically substituted compound NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ. In the Se-doped system, substitutional disorder is present and can significantly modify the transport properties and apparent critical behavior. By contrast, pressure tuning preserves the crystallographic and chemical cleanliness of the parent compound, making it possible to isolate the effects of quantum critical antiferromagnetic fluctuations. The comparison shows that disorder is not a minor perturbation but can drastically alter the nature of the metallic state near the quantum critical point, including the observed resistivity exponent and the scale at which Fermi-liquid behavior re-emerges.

Overall, the study establishes clean NiS₂ under pressure as an important model system for examining antiferromagnetic quantum criticality in a correlated metal. The persistence of T³ᐟ² resistivity and the severe suppression of the Fermi-liquid crossover provide strong evidence for robust non-Fermi-liquid transport near the pressure-induced quantum critical point. These findings highlight the central role of sample purity and tuning method in determining the observed properties of quantum critical materials.
outputs.L5:
Under high-pressure conditions measured in **GPa**, materials can undergo dramatic changes in their electronic, magnetic, and structural properties. One important concept in condensed matter physics is the **QCP**, or quantum critical point, which occurs at absolute zero temperature when a continuous phase transition is driven by a non-thermal parameter such as pressure, magnetic field, or chemical composition.

Pressure is often a powerful tuning tool because increasing it by several **GPa** can change the spacing between atoms, modify electron interactions, and even create new phases of matter. Near a **QCP**, a material may display unusual behavior, such as non-Fermi-liquid transport, enhanced fluctuations, or the emergence of superconductivity.

The symbol **Omega** (Ω) is commonly associated with electrical resistance, measured in ohms. In experiments near a QCP, researchers often track changes in resistivity, reported in Ω or related units, as pressure is increased. A sudden or unusual change in resistance under several GPa can indicate that the system is approaching a quantum phase transition.

Together, **QCP**, **GPa**, and **Omega** represent key ideas in high-pressure quantum materials research: the search for critical phases, the use of pressure as a tuning parameter, and the measurement of electrical response to reveal new states of matter.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract-style summary of a study on pressure-induced quantum criticality in clean NiS₂ pyrite single crystals, emphasizing resistivity behavior and comparison with disordered NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ.
counterfactuals.output:
We report a pressure-tuning study of quantum critical transport in high-quality single crystals of pyrite NiS₂, a clean bandwidth-controlled Mott system. Electrical resistivity measurements under hydrostatic pressure reveal a continuous suppression of the antiferromagnetic insulating state and the emergence of a metallic ground state above a critical pressure. Near the critical pressure, the low-temperature resistivity deviates strongly from conventional Fermi-liquid behavior: instead of the usual ρ(T) = ρ₀ + AT² form, the data are described over an extended temperature range by a non-Fermi-liquid power law, ρ(T) = ρ₀ + ATⁿ, with n significantly below 2. Upon moving further into the metallic phase, Fermi-liquid T² behavior is gradually recovered, indicating that the anomalous scattering is confined to the vicinity of the pressure-induced quantum critical regime.

The use of stoichiometric NiS₂ single crystals provides an important contrast to chemically substituted NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ, where bandwidth control is achieved by Se substitution but inevitably introduces quenched disorder. While both pressure-tuned NiS₂ and Se-substituted NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ exhibit suppression of insulating antiferromagnetism and anomalous metallic transport near the metal-insulator boundary, the clean pressure-tuned system displays sharper critical behavior and lower residual resistivity. This comparison suggests that the non-Fermi-liquid resistivity is intrinsic to the Mott/antiferromagnetic quantum critical point rather than a disorder-driven effect, although disorder in NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ broadens the transition and modifies the apparent transport exponents.

These results establish clean NiS₂ under pressure as a model platform for studying bandwidth-controlled quantum criticality near a Mott transition. The observed evolution from insulating behavior to anomalous metallic transport and finally to a Fermi-liquid state highlights the central role of critical spin and charge fluctuations in governing electron scattering near the pressure-induced quantum critical point.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the experimental findings for a quantum critical point between antiferromagnetic and paramagnetic phases in NiS₂ under hydrostatic pressure around 7 GPa.
counterfactuals.output:
Experiments on **NiS₂ under nearly hydrostatic pressure** show a pressure-tuned quantum phase transition near **\(p_c \approx 7\) GPa** between an antiferromagnetic state and a paramagnetic metal.

Key findings:

- **Suppression of antiferromagnetism:**  
  At lower pressures NiS₂ is antiferromagnetic, with a Néel temperature \(T_N\). Increasing pressure steadily lowers \(T_N\), and it extrapolates to zero at about **7 GPa**, indicating an antiferromagnetic quantum critical point.

- **Metallic state near the critical pressure:**  
  Pressure first drives NiS₂ from an insulating/Mott-like state into a metal, and the antiferromagnetic phase persists into the metallic regime before disappearing at \(p_c\).

- **Non-Fermi-liquid transport at the critical point:**  
  Around \(p_c\), the low-temperature resistivity does not follow the ordinary Fermi-liquid form  
  \[
  \rho(T)=\rho_0+AT^2 .
  \]  
  Instead, it is well described by an anomalous power law close to  
  \[
  \rho(T)=\rho_0+AT^{3/2},
  \]  
  which is characteristic of scattering from critical antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations in a three-dimensional metal.

- **Recovery of Fermi-liquid behavior away from \(p_c\):**  
  On the paramagnetic side at pressures above roughly 7 GPa, the resistivity gradually returns to the conventional  
  \[
  \rho \sim T^2
  \]  
  behavior at low temperature, consistent with a Landau Fermi liquid.

- **Enhanced scattering near the QCP:**  
  The coefficient of the temperature-dependent resistivity is enhanced near the critical pressure, reflecting strong magnetic fluctuations.

Overall, the experiments identify NiS₂ as a pressure-tuned system where antiferromagnetic order is continuously suppressed to zero temperature near **7 GPa**, producing a **quantum critical point** with pronounced non-Fermi-liquid transport before a paramagnetic Fermi-liquid metal is recovered at higher pressure.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize how disorder affects quantum critical behavior in NiS₂ by comparing clean pressure-tuned NiS₂ with the solid-solution system NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ.
counterfactuals.output:
Disorder changes the NiS₂ quantum critical problem from a relatively clean bandwidth-tuned antiferromagnetic/Mott system into a chemically disordered, inhomogeneous critical system.

### Clean pressure-tuned NiS₂
- Applying hydrostatic pressure tunes the bandwidth without changing the lattice chemistry, so it is a comparatively “clean” control parameter.
- The suppression of antiferromagnetic order and the approach to the metallic quantum critical regime are relatively sharp.
- Transport and thermodynamics can be interpreted more directly in terms of a clean quantum critical point, often compared with itinerant antiferromagnetic spin-fluctuation behavior.
- Non-Fermi-liquid behavior appears near the critical pressure, while Fermi-liquid behavior is recovered away from the critical region.
- Because pressure does not introduce substantial random potential scattering, residual resistivity remains lower and critical scaling is less obscured.

### NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ solid solution
- Replacing S with Se also increases bandwidth, acting like “chemical pressure,” but it simultaneously introduces substitutional disorder.
- Random S/Se occupation produces spatial variations in local bandwidth, exchange interactions, and local proximity to the metal-insulator or magnetic transition.
- As a result, the transition is broadened compared with pressure-tuned NiS₂.
- Disorder enhances residual resistivity and can mask or modify intrinsic quantum critical scaling.
- Instead of a single uniform critical point, the system may show inhomogeneous behavior, with locally metallic or magnetically ordered regions appearing before the bulk transition.
- Rare-region or Griffiths-like effects can extend non-Fermi-liquid behavior over a wider composition range than expected for a clean quantum critical point.

### Overall comparison
Pressure-tuned NiS₂ is closer to a clean quantum critical system, where the collapse of antiferromagnetism and associated non-Fermi-liquid transport can be tied to intrinsic critical fluctuations. In NiS₂₋ₓSeₓ, Se substitution tunes the same basic bandwidth-controlled physics but adds quenched disorder, which broadens the transition, increases scattering, promotes spatial inhomogeneity, and can alter the apparent critical exponents or even the universality class. Thus, disorder does not merely shift the critical point; it qualitatively changes how quantum criticality is observed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a concise scientific abstract about non-Fermi liquid resistivity in clean NiS₂ near a pressure-induced quantum critical point, including values for pressure, residual resistivity, and temperature dependence.
counterfactuals.output:
We report non-Fermi-liquid charge transport in clean single-crystal NiS₂ tuned through its pressure-induced magnetic quantum critical point. Hydrostatic pressure suppresses antiferromagnetic order to a critical pressure \(p_c \approx 76\) kbar (\(\sim 7.6\) GPa), where the low-temperature resistivity departs strongly from the Fermi-liquid form. Near \(p_c\), samples with very low residual resistivity, \(\rho_0 \approx 0.5\)–\(1\,\mu\Omega\,\text{cm}\), exhibit

\[
\rho(T)=\rho_0 + A T^n,
\]

with \(n \approx 1.5\) over an extended low-temperature range, rather than the conventional \(T^2\) dependence expected for a Fermi liquid. Away from the critical pressure, \(T^2\) behavior is recovered, indicating restoration of coherent quasiparticle scattering. The observation of robust \(T^{3/2}\) resistivity in a very clean metal near \(p_c\) is consistent with enhanced scattering from critical antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations and identifies pressurized NiS₂ as a model system for studying non-Fermi-liquid transport at an itinerant quantum critical point.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: What happens to the resistivity and Fermi-liquid crossover temperature in clean NiS₂ pyrite single crystals when hydrostatic pressure up to 9 GPa is applied near the antiferromagnetic-paramagnetic quantum critical point?
counterfactuals.output:
In clean pyrite NiS₂ single crystals under hydrostatic pressure, the system is driven from an antiferromagnetic state toward a paramagnetic metal near a pressure-tuned quantum critical point, around several GPa.

Near the antiferromagnetic–paramagnetic quantum critical point:

- The low-temperature resistivity no longer follows the conventional Fermi-liquid form  
  \[
  \rho(T)=\rho_0+AT^2 .
  \]
- Instead, it shows non-Fermi-liquid behavior, approximately  
  \[
  \rho(T)-\rho_0 \propto T^{3/2},
  \]
  over an extended temperature range.
- The Fermi-liquid crossover temperature \(T_{\mathrm{FL}}\), below which \(T^2\) resistivity is recovered, is strongly suppressed as the critical pressure is approached.
- At or very near the quantum critical point, \(T_{\mathrm{FL}}\) becomes very small, effectively tending toward zero within the experimental temperature window.
- On the paramagnetic side at higher pressures, e.g. approaching 9 GPa, conventional Fermi-liquid behavior re-emerges at low temperature and \(T_{\mathrm{FL}}\) increases again.

So, pressure drives NiS₂ into a quantum critical regime where resistivity becomes anomalous/non-Fermi-liquid-like, while the Fermi-liquid crossover temperature collapses near the critical pressure and recovers away from it.
